area: Area V. Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how a chandelle trades airspeed for altitude while turning, and fly one each way to commercial standards: about 30° of bank, constant bank and rising pitch to the 90° point, constant pitch and a constant-rate rollout to the 180° point (±10°), finishing just above a stall airspeed, no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.
why: A chandelle is a maximum performance 180° climbing turn that ends wings level, nose high, just above stall speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. It teaches you to manage energy, to keep the airplane coordinated as the speed runs out and the left-turning tendencies build, and to recognize how close you are to a stall at low airspeed and high power [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

prereading.what: The chandelle: the two halves, entry, power, rudder in left and right chandelles, the finish, and the common errors. Read this twice.
prereading.label: AFH 10-4 to 10-6

prereading.what: Energy management: total mechanical energy, thrust minus drag, energy exchange, and the throttle and elevator as energy controls.
prereading.label: AFH 4-1 to 4-4

prereading.what: Climbs and climbing turns: types of climb, P-factor and torque in the climb, pitch as speed decays, why steep banks hurt climb performance.
prereading.label: AFH 3-17 to 3-20

prereading.what: Lift in a turn, adverse yaw and the rudder, slip and skid, rate and radius of turn, overbanking tendency.
prereading.label: AFH 3-12 to 3-14

prereading.what: The four parts of 'torque': torque reaction, corkscrew slipstream, gyroscopic action and P-factor.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-30 to 5-32

prereading.what: Maneuvering speed, load factor and stall speed, and the PHAK's short section on chandelles and lazy eights.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-35 to 5-37

prereading.what: Accelerated stalls, VA and VO and weight, and the cross-control stall.
prereading.label: AFH 5-19 to 5-20

warmup: Think first: you start a chandelle at about 105 knots and finish half a turn later just above the stall, a few hundred feet higher. The engine was at climb power the whole time. Where did the altitude come from: the engine, the airspeed you started with, or both? And what would happen if you used up all the airspeed at the 120° point instead of the 180° point?

key_terms.def: A maximum performance 180° climbing turn that starts from about straight-and-level flight and ends wings level, nose high, just above stall speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
The half of the chandelle flown at a constant bank with a continuously increasing pitch attitude [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
The half flown at a constant pitch attitude with a continuously decreasing bank, a slow constant-rate rollout to wings level at 180° [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

The highest speed at which the design limit load can be reached by gusts or by full deflection of one control without structural damage. It goes down as weight goes down [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
An older limitation on some airplanes: the highest speed at which, at any weight, full control travel will not exceed the design limit load [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
A stall at more than 1 G, as in a turn or a pull-up, so it happens at a higher indicated airspeed than the 1 G stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

In a tighter turn the outside wing flies faster and makes more lift, so the bank tends to steepen unless you hold opposite aileron [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. In a chandelle it grows as the airspeed drops [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
At a high angle of attack the downward-moving propeller blade takes a bigger bite than the upward-moving one, which yaws the nose to the left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
The spiraling slipstream strikes the vertical fin and yaws the airplane. It is strongest at high propeller speed and low forward speed [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
When you roll with aileron, the rising wing gets more lift and more drag, so the nose yaws away from the direction of the roll [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].
The airplane's energy stored as altitude (potential energy) plus its energy stored as airspeed (kinetic energy) [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].
Trading airspeed for altitude or altitude for airspeed with the elevator. When energy is exchanged, the two always change in opposite directions [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].

body.p: A chandelle is a maximum performance, 180° climbing turn. It starts from about straight-and-level flight and ends with the wings level, the nose high, and the airspeed just above the stall [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. The goal is to gain as much altitude as possible for the bank and power you chose. But you are not graded on the altitude you gain. You are graded on how well you get the most climb out of that bank and power, and on your skill [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

head: What the examiner checks
Commercial ACS standard
rows: Select an altitude that allows the maneuver to be performed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.C.S2)
Establish the appropriate entry configuration, power, and airspeed (ACS CA.V.C.S3)
Establish the angle of bank at approximately 30° (ACS CA.V.C.S4)
Simultaneously apply power and pitch to maintain a smooth, coordinated climbing turn, in either direction, to the 90° point, with a constant bank and continuously decreasing airspeed (ACS CA.V.C.S5)
Coordinated constant rate rollout from the 90° point to the 180° point, maintaining power and a constant pitch attitude (ACS CA.V.C.S6)
Complete the rollout at the 180° point, ±10°, just above a stall airspeed, and hold that airspeed momentarily, avoiding a stall (ACS CA.V.C.S7)
Resume straight-and-level flight with minimum loss of altitude (ACS CA.V.C.S8)

body.p: Notice what the standard leaves out. There is no altitude-gain target, no airspeed number for the finish and no pitch attitude. The only numbers are about 30° of bank, ±10° on the 180° point and 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.C.S2, S4, S7). The rest is judged on smoothness, coordination and energy planning.

callout.text: For an initial commercial ASEL applicant, the examiner picks Chandelles or Lazy Eights (ACS Appendix 3, Area V). Prepare both.
First half: bank fixed, nose coming up. Second half: nose fixed, bank coming out. Finish: wings level, slow, not stalled.

check.q: What three numbers does the commercial ACS give for the chandelle?
check.a: About 30° of bank (S4), the 180° point within ±10° (S7), and no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (S2) (ACS CA.V.C).

chunks.title: Two halves: constant bank, then constant pitch

body.p: The AFH splits the chandelle into two 90° parts. In the first 90°, the bank stays constant and the pitch keeps increasing. In the second 90°, the pitch stays constant and the bank keeps decreasing [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

bullets: First 90°: set the bank, add power, and raise the pitch attitude at a rate that puts the highest pitch exactly at the 90° point [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
At the 90° point: the highest pitch attitude is then held for the rest of the maneuver [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
Second 90°: holding that pitch, begin a slow, coordinated, constant-rate rollout so the wings come level at the 180° point [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
Finish: wings level, airspeed just above the power-on stall speed, and the nose-high attitude held for a moment [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

body.p: The pitch you reach at 90° decides the end of the maneuver. Set it too low and the airspeed never comes down to just above the stall. Set it too high and the airplane may stall before you finish [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. The rollout rate decides the heading. Roll out too fast or too slowly and you either turn past 180° or do not finish the turn as the wings come level [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

Application: in the second half the airspeed is still dropping while the pitch attitude is fixed. That is why the second 90° needs a planned, steady rollout. You are spending the last of the airspeed while you take out the bank.

callout.text: Pick a reference on the horizon off your wingtip before you start. It marks the 90° point. A second reference behind you marks the 180° point.

check.q: At the 90° point, what stops changing and what starts changing?
check.a: The pitch attitude stops changing (it is held from here) and the bank starts coming out in a constant-rate rollout [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

chunks.title: Entry: configuration, speed and power for a maximum performance climb

body.p: Before the chandelle, the flaps and the landing gear (if retractable) go up. Enter from straight-and-level flight or a shallow dive at the manufacturer's recommended airspeed. In many airplanes that is VA or VO [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. The PHAK agrees that the recommended entry speed is generally near the design maneuvering speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

bullets: Roll smoothly into a coordinated turn to the bank you want, generally 30° [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
Then start the climbing turn: smooth back elevator pressure at a constant rate while you add power to the recommended setting [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
Fixed-pitch propeller: set the throttle so you do not exceed the rpm limits [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
Constant-speed propeller: power may be set at the normal cruise or climb setting, as appropriate [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
With a controllable-pitch propeller, advance the propeller control before increasing power [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

body.p: Why only 30° of bank? In any climbing turn some of the lift turns the airplane, so the climb is shallower than a straight climb. Steep banks cut the rate of climb a lot, and with a medium or steep bank, climb performance is degraded or may be gone [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. The chandelle's moderate bank is a trade between turning 180° and still climbing.

A normally aspirated engine loses power as you climb into thinner air. With a fixed-pitch propeller you see the rpm drop; you keep advancing the throttle to hold the climb setting [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Application: a high density altitude day means less excess power and a smaller altitude gain.

callout.text: Look up the POH entry speed and VA for today's weight before the flight. VA goes down when the airplane is lighter [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

check.q: Your airplane has a constant-speed propeller. What power does the AFH say to use in the chandelle?
check.a: Normal cruise or climb power, as appropriate [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

chunks.title: Maneuvering speed, the pull-up and accelerated stalls

body.p: The chandelle begins fast and with a pull-up, so think about structure and stalls at the start, not just at the end. At or below VA or VO, the airplane reaches the critical angle of attack and stalls, unloading the wing, before it can exceed the design load limit. Above them it can reach the limit load before it stalls [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

VA is not one fixed number. It must be considered with weight: for example 100 knots heavily loaded but only 90 knots with a light load [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. VA protects you for a single full control input in one axis, one time, in smooth air. It does not protect against several full inputs in one axis or full inputs in more than one axis at once [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

Load factor is about technique too. The better a chandelle is flown, the lower the load factor. A pull-up of more than 2 G will not gain as much altitude, and in a low-powered airplane it may give a net loss. The smoothest pull-up, with a moderate load factor, gains the most [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

An accelerated stall is any stall above 1 G. It happens at a higher indicated airspeed than the 1 G stall, for example in turns, pull-ups or other abrupt changes in flightpath [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Stalling speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. Application: a level 30° bank is about 1.15 G, which raises the stall speed by about 7.5 percent. A hard pull adds more.

callout.text: Stalls from abrupt maneuvers tend to be more aggressive than 1 G stalls and can come at a higher speed or lower pitch than you expect. Without an immediate recovery they can lead to a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Smooth pull, moderate G, more altitude. Yank, more G, less altitude and a stall waiting.

check.q: Why does a hard pull-up at the start of a chandelle cost altitude instead of gaining it?
check.a: A pull-up above about 2 G will not gain as much altitude and in a low-powered airplane may give a net loss; the smoothest pull-up with a moderate load factor gains the most [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

chunks.title: Energy management: where the altitude comes from

body.p: The airplane's total mechanical energy is its potential energy from altitude plus its kinetic energy from airspeed, written mgh + ½mV² [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. Thrust adds energy and drag takes it away. When thrust is more than drag, total energy grows, and you choose whether to store it as altitude or airspeed [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].

The AFH gives each control an energy job. The throttle is the total energy controller. The elevator is the energy distribution controller: it moves energy between the altitude tank and the airspeed tank. Neither one controls altitude or airspeed by itself [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

A chandelle uses both jobs at once. You add power, so the throttle adds total energy (thrust greater than drag). At the same time you raise the nose, so the elevator moves energy out of airspeed into altitude. To trade speed for altitude, pitch up [[24:96|AFH 4-10]]. When energy is exchanged, altitude goes up as airspeed comes down [[24:88|AFH 4-2]]. Row F of the figure shows a pure exchange; the chandelle adds engine energy on top of it.

Why it is a risk item: mismanaging altitude and airspeed is a factor in the three most common types of fatal accidents, loss of control in flight, controlled flight into terrain, and approach-and-landing accidents. Energy management also aims to prevent an irreversible deceleration or sink rate [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. In a chandelle you deliberately spend nearly all of your airspeed. If the plan is off, the airspeed runs out before the turn does.

callout.text: Your energy reference is indicated altitude and indicated airspeed, not height above the ground or groundspeed [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. Rising terrain under a chandelle eats your margin even when the altimeter climbs.
Throttle fills the tanks. Elevator pours speed into height. A chandelle does both, and ends with the speed tank almost empty.

check.q: In energy terms, what do the throttle and the elevator each do in a chandelle?
check.a: The throttle adds total energy (thrust more than drag); the elevator distributes it, trading airspeed for altitude by pitching up [[24:90|AFH 4-4]] [[24:96|AFH 4-10]].

chunks.title: Left-turning tendencies as the airspeed runs out

body.p: To the pilot, 'torque' is four things: torque reaction from the engine and propeller, the corkscrewing slipstream, gyroscopic action of the propeller, and asymmetric loading of the propeller (P-factor) [[1:127|PHAK 5-30]] [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. A chandelle builds the worst case for most of them: high power, a high angle of attack and a speed that keeps falling.

P-factor: at a high angle of attack the downward-moving blade takes a bigger bite, the center of thrust moves to the right, and the nose yaws left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]. In a climb, torque also rolls the airplane left, so right rudder and some aileron pressure are needed [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

Corkscrew effect: at high propeller speed and low forward speed, the spiraling slipstream is compact and pushes hard on the vertical fin. As speed increases the spiral stretches out and the effect weakens [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. Built-in compensation for torque is generally set for cruising speed, where the airplane spends most of its time [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. Application: at chandelle speeds it does less and less for you.

The AFH puts it plainly: as airspeed decreases in a chandelle, left-turning tendencies such as P-factor have greater effect, so right rudder pressure is progressively increased to stay coordinated [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Near the critical angle of attack the controls are also less effective, and the closer you are to the 1 G stall, the more right rudder it takes [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

callout.text: Keep feeding in right rudder as the speed bleeds off. Feel for slipping or skidding, glance at the ball, and use the control pressure it takes [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

check.q: Why does the chandelle need more and more right rudder as it goes on?
check.a: Airspeed keeps dropping at high power and a rising angle of attack, so P-factor and the other left-turning tendencies have more effect [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

chunks.title: Coordination: left and right chandelles are different

body.p: Coordination means rudder with aileron to cancel adverse yaw. When you deflect the ailerons, the rising wing gets more lift and drag, so the nose yaws away from the roll. Rudder in the direction of the roll cancels it [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. In a skid you feel pushed to the outside of the turn; in a slip, to the inside [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].

head: Rollout from
What yaws the nose
Rudder the AFH describes
rows: Rolling right gives left adverse yaw, added to left-turning tendencies such as P-factor
Significant right rudder near the end [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]
Rolling left gives a yawing moment to the right, which partly cancels the left-turning tendency
Very little left rudder or less right rudder, depending on the airplane [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]

body.p: So the same maneuver needs different feet each way. At the slowest point near the finish of a left chandelle, the right rudder pressure is significant [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. In a right chandelle, the rollout itself helps you, and you may need to relax right rudder.

callout.text: Holding uncoordinated control deflections can set up a spin, especially at low altitude [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. A cross-control stall can come with very little warning and roll the airplane toward inverted [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Slow, nose high and uncoordinated is exactly that setup.
The ACS lets you fly it in either direction (ACS CA.V.C.S5). Practice both, so the examiner's choice does not surprise your feet.

check.q: Rolling out of a right chandelle, why might you need less right rudder than in a left one?
check.a: Rolling out to the left makes a yawing moment to the right that partly cancels the left-turning tendencies [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

body.p: In a turn the outside wing travels a longer path than the inside wing in the same time, so it is faster and makes more lift. That makes the bank tend to steepen, and you hold it with opposite aileron [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. As the radius gets smaller, the speed difference between the wings grows [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

A 30° bank is usually a medium bank, where the airplane tends to hold its bank on its own [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. But the chandelle is not normal. The AFH warns that as airspeed decreases, the overbanking tendency increases, so proper use of the ailerons keeps the bank at a fixed angle until the rollout starts at the 90° point [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

Letting the bank grow after you set it is a listed common error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. It hurts in two ways. A steeper bank turns the airplane faster, so you reach 90° early with speed to spare. And a steeper bank cuts climb performance [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

callout.text: Check the bank on the attitude indicator once early in the turn, then hold the same sight picture of the wing and the horizon. Expect to hold a little opposite aileron as the speed drops.

check.q: Why does the overbanking tendency get stronger as the chandelle goes on?
check.a: It increases as airspeed decreases, so aileron is needed to keep the bank fixed until the 90° point [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

chunks.title: Pitch control as the speed decays, and stall awareness at the finish

body.p: Holding a pitch attitude while the airspeed falls is not 'set and forget'. As airspeed decreases in a climb, the pitch attitude tends to drop unless you increase elevator pressure [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. In the second 90° of the chandelle, the rollout gives you more vertical lift, but the speed keeps falling, so a slight increase of back pressure is still needed to keep the pitch from decreasing [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

bullets: First 90°: back pressure at a constant rate so the pitch rises smoothly to its highest point at 90° [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
Second 90°: no more pitch increase; letting the pitch rise as the bank comes out is a listed error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].
But do not let the nose sag either: a slight extra back pressure holds the attitude as speed drops [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
Near the stall, the elevator is less responsive and larger control movements are needed [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

body.p: The finish is the most delicate moment. Wings level at the 180° point, the airspeed just above the power-on stall speed, and the nose-high attitude held only momentarily [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. The ACS says just above a stall airspeed, held momentarily, avoiding a stall (ACS CA.V.C.S7). Stalling at any point is a listed error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

callout.text: If a stall does start, recover right away: forward elevator pressure to reduce the angle of attack and stop the stall warning, level the wings with aileron, coordinate with rudder, and adjust power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Learn the sounds and feel near the end: quieter airflow, light controls, lots of right rudder. Know your airplane's power-on stall speed from the POH so you know what 'just above' looks like.

check.q: During the second 90°, the pitch is supposed to stay constant. Why do you still need a little more back pressure?
check.a: The airspeed keeps decreasing, so without a slight increase in back pressure the pitch attitude would drop [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

chunks.title: Rate and radius of turn, and confined areas

body.p: At a given bank, a slower airspeed gives a smaller turn radius and a faster rate of turn [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. The formulas use true airspeed: rate of turn equals 1,091 times the tangent of the bank divided by airspeed in knots, and radius equals airspeed squared divided by 11.26 times the tangent of the bank [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. Double the speed at the same bank and the radius is four times as large [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].

Application to the chandelle: during the first 90° the bank is fixed while the speed falls, so the circle keeps tightening. Worked from the PHAK formula at 30° of bank, about 1,700 feet of radius at 105 knots TAS shrinks to about 550 feet at 60 knots TAS.

The PHAK canyon example: at 30° of bank, the airplane at 120 knots needs about 4,000 feet to reverse course and makes it; the one at 140 knots needs over 6,000 feet and hits the wall. Airspeed is the most influential factor in how much room a turn needs, and many pilots have steepened the bank when slowing down would have been better [[1:138|PHAK 5-41]].

Application: a chandelle looks like a way out of a valley, but it ends at nearly zero excess airspeed, nose high, in a tight space. A planned slow-down and a moderate bank give a small radius with far more margin. Practice chandelles in open air, well away from terrain.

callout.text: When faced with rising terrain, the AFH suggests managing energy to maximize gains and minimize losses, and also says a safer heading may be an option [[24:88|AFH 4-2]]. Turn away early, not with a last-moment, all-energy maneuver.

check.q: In the first 90° of a chandelle the bank is fixed. What happens to the turn radius as the airspeed drops?
check.a: It gets smaller and the rate of turn increases, because at a given bank a slower airspeed gives a smaller radius [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

chunks.title: Clearing, altitude and division of attention

body.p: Start every chandelle by clearing the airspace for traffic and hazards [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. The PHAK says clearing procedures should come before all turns, chandelles included, and urges pilots to say the calls out loud: 'clear' left, right, above, or below. In a high-wing airplane, raise the wing in the direction of the turn and look; in a low wing, lower it [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]].

bullets: Scan in eye movements of no more than 10°, looking at each area for at least 1 second [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Clearing plus good scanning is the most effective strategy for collision avoidance [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
Traffic clusters along airways, near VORs and in airport surface areas, and most collisions happen in good weather [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
A target with no relative motion that only grows larger is on a collision course; take evasive action [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

body.p: Altitude: pick one that keeps the whole maneuver no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.C.S2). Figure 10-3 shows the same floor at the entry [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. The entry is the lowest point, and a shallow-dive entry [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] starts a little lower still. Application: check the terrain under the whole half circle, not just under you.

Division of attention: you hold a bank, build pitch, add power and rudder, watch two references, and keep scanning, all as the speed drops. Not scanning for traffic and flying by the instruments instead of outside references are both on the AFH error list [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. In visual conditions your eyes are the main orientation source and usually beat false sensations from the body [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]. An abrupt head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn can cause the Coriolis illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

callout.text: Priority in the maneuver: outside attitude first, a quick look at airspeed and the ball second, then the traffic scan. A radio call or a checklist can wait until you are back in level flight.

check.q: The terrain is 1,400 feet MSL. What is the lowest altitude the chandelle may reach?
check.a: 2,900 feet MSL: 1,400 + 1,500 = 2,900, so the maneuver stays no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.C.S2).

body.p: A generic flow from the AFH. Your POH gives the real entry speed, power and limits.

bullets: 1. Flaps and gear up. Clear the area (ACS CA.V.C.S1) [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
2. Pick an altitude that keeps you at or above 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.C.S2) [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
3. Establish the POH entry speed (often VA or VO) in straight-and-level flight or a shallow dive [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
4. Note a reference off the wingtip (90° point) and behind you (180° point).
5. Roll smoothly and coordinated to about 30° of bank (ACS CA.V.C.S4) [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
6. Smooth back pressure at a constant rate while adding power to the recommended setting; do not exceed rpm limits [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
7. Hold the bank constant with aileron against overbanking; add right rudder as the speed falls [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
8. Reach the highest pitch exactly at the 90° point [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
9. Hold that pitch and begin a slow, constant-rate, coordinated rollout; a slight back pressure keeps the nose from dropping [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
10. Wings level at the 180° point (±10°), just above stall speed; hold it momentarily (ACS CA.V.C.S7) [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
11. Lower the nose smoothly to straight-and-level flight with minimum altitude loss, then set cruise power (ACS CA.V.C.S8) [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

body.p: Leaving the maneuver: once the airplane is in controlled flight, reduce the pitch and return to cruise [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. The AFH's level-off advice applies: lower the pitch smoothly and slowly so the airspeed can build. A pitch change that is too fast, before the airspeed increases, can cost altitude [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

callout.text: Clear, speed, 30, pull and power, hold the bank, 90 freeze the nose, roll out slow, 180 wings level, ease it down.

check.q: You start a right chandelle on heading 120. On what heading should the wings come level, and what range passes?

body.p: The AFH lists 14 common errors [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. Most of them come from three things: the wrong bank, the wrong pitch, or the wrong timing at the 90° point.

head: AFH common error
What it does
Fix
rows: 30°, not more; steep banks degrade the climb [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]
Bank increases after it is set
Pitch and heading plan falls apart
Use a wingtip reference for the 90° point
Airspeed well above stall at the end [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]
Smooth inputs; ball centered with right rudder as speed falls [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]
Correct pitch plan; recover at once [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Steep turn instead of a climbing maneuver
Pitch and power, not just bank
No traffic scan; flying by instruments

body.p: Table source: the chandelle common error list [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]; fixes as cited. Application: why does a too-shallow bank lead to a stall? With less bank the airplane turns more slowly, so the speed is gone before the heading reaches 180°.

callout.text: If the speed is nearly gone and the heading is still short of 180°, do not hold the nose up to make the heading. Lower the nose and accept the error. A stall is a bigger error than a heading miss (ACS CA.V.C.S7) [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].
Debrief each one with three numbers: bank held, heading at wings level, and airspeed at the finish compared with the stall speed.

check.q: Your chandelle ends with wings level at 180° but the airspeed is 20 knots above the stall. What went wrong?
check.a: The pitch attitude was too low, so the airspeed never decayed to just above the stall [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

f1.caption: Figure 10-3. Chandelle. (AFH 10-5)
f1.alt: A high-wing airplane flies a climbing 180° turn over farmland toward hills, shown at five lettered points. A: level entry, with a box listing clear area, VA, VO or manufacturer's speed, no lower than 1,500 feet AGL, trim. B: rolled into a bank, with a box listing roll into 30° bank, neutralize ailerons, begin increasing pitch toward climbing attitude, apply full power without exceeding limits, increase rudder pressure. C: banked and nose high, with a box saying maintain 30° bank until this point then begin gradual rollout, and maximum pitch should be reached, no further changes in pitch. D: shallower bank, box says continue smooth rollout, hold pitch, maintain coordinated flight. E: wings level and nose high, box says complete rollout to wings level at the 180° point, airspeed VS1, maintain coordinated flight, hold airspeed without stalling.

f2.caption: Figure 4-3. The reservoir analogy illustrating the primary role of the throttle and elevator to manage the airplane's energy state. (AFH 4-4)
f2.alt: A pipe diagram. Energy gain enters on the left through a valve labeled throttle as thrust, and energy loss leaves on the right as drag. A vertical pipe labeled net energy flow, thrust minus drag, leads down to a valve labeled elevator that connects two tanks: Altitude (potential energy) on the left and Airspeed (kinetic energy) on the right, with arrows showing flow both ways between them.

f3.caption: Figure 4-1 A-F. Examples of typical energy transactions. (AFH 4-2)
f3.alt: A table of six rows, A to F, each with a small two-tank drawing. Columns give net energy change (thrust minus drag), change in stored altitude and airspeed, and the result. A: greater than zero, altitude up, climb at constant airspeed. B: greater than zero, airspeed up, acceleration at constant altitude. C: less than zero, altitude down, descent at constant airspeed. D: less than zero, airspeed down, deceleration at constant altitude. E: zero, no change, constant altitude and airspeed. F: zero, altitude up and airspeed down, climb and deceleration.

f4.caption: Figure 5-51. Asymmetrical loading of propeller (P-factor). (PHAK 5-33)
f4.alt: Two side views of the nose of a high-wing airplane. Left, low angle of attack: the arrows for the load on the upward moving and downward moving propeller blades are equal. Right, high angle of attack with the nose raised: the arrow for the downward moving blade is much longer than the one for the upward moving blade.

f5.caption: Figure 5-48. Corkscrewing slipstream. (PHAK 5-31)
f5.alt: A low-wing airplane seen from above and behind. An orange band labeled slipstream spirals around the fuselage from the propeller and strikes the left side of the vertical fin, where an arrow is labeled force. A blue curved arrow at the nose is labeled yaw, and another curved arrow circles the tail.

f6.caption: Figure 3-15. Overbanking tendency. (AFH 3-14)
f6.alt: A high-wing airplane in a steep bank against the sky. A box at the raised outer wing says it travels a greater distance, with higher speed and more lift. A box at the lowered inner wing says it travels a shorter distance, with lower speed and less lift. A large curved arrow shows the bank tending to steepen.

f7.caption: Figure 5-62. Two aircraft have flown into a canyon by error. The canyon is 5,000 feet across. At 120 knots and 30° of bank one reverses course in about 4,000 feet; at 140 knots and 30° the other needs over 6,000 feet and hits the wall. (PHAK 5-41)
f7.alt: Two aerial photos of a canyon with a 5,000 foot wide bar between the cliffs. Top, 120 knots: a green turn path with a 2,215 foot radius and 4,430 foot diameter fits inside the canyon, with the formula R equals 120 squared over 11.26 times 0.5773 equals 2,215 feet. Bottom, 140 knots: a red path with a 3,014 foot radius and 6,028 foot diameter runs past the canyon wall, with R equals 140 squared over 11.26 times 0.5773 equals 3,014 feet. Each panel shows an airspeed indicator and an attitude indicator in a 30° bank.

scenario.title: Chandelles over the foothills on checkride day
scenario.setup: You are flying a high-wing trainer with a fixed-pitch propeller on a warm afternoon for your commercial checkride. You are light: two people and half fuel. The practice area sits over rolling farmland at about 1,300 feet MSL that rises to low hills to the east. A flight school's trainers also use the area. The examiner asks for a left chandelle, then a right one.

questions.q: What is the lowest altitude your chandelle may reach, and where will that point be?
questions.a: 1,300 + 1,500 = 2,800 feet MSL (ACS CA.V.C.S2). The entry is the lowest point, and a shallow-dive entry starts lower still [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Check the terrain under the whole turn, including the hills to the east.

questions.q: What entry speed do you choose, given that you are light today?
questions.a: The manufacturer's recommended speed, which in many airplanes is VA or VO [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. VA goes down as weight goes down [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]], so a max-weight VA is too fast at today's weight.

questions.q: How do you clear the area before rolling in?
questions.a: Clearing turns [[24:33|AFH 1-12]], raising the wing in the direction of the turn to look, and saying 'clear left, right, above, below' out loud [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]]. Scan in steps of 10° or less, at least 1 second each [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

questions.q: It is warm and the rpm sags as you climb through the first 90°. What do you do, and what does it mean for altitude gain?
questions.a: Keep advancing the throttle to hold the climb setting without exceeding the rpm limits [[24:80|AFH 3-19]] [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Less excess power means less altitude gained, but you are judged on performance for the power available, not the gain [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

questions.q: Near the end of the left chandelle the airplane is yawing left and you feel pushed to one side. What is happening and what is the fix?
questions.a: Left adverse yaw from the rollout plus P-factor at low speed; it needs significant right rudder [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Uncoordinated flight at low speed sets up a cross-control stall and spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

questions.q: On the debrief the examiner asks why you would not use a chandelle to escape a narrow valley. What do you say?
questions.a: It ends just above the stall with almost no spare energy [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Airspeed is the biggest factor in how much room a turn needs, so slowing down with a moderate bank is the better choice [[1:138|PHAK 5-41]]. Turning toward a safer heading early is part of energy management [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].

skills.do: Clear the area before the maneuver.
skills.practice: Clearing turns before every chandelle, with the wing raised or lowered to look and the calls said out loud [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]].

skills.do: Pick an altitude so the whole maneuver stays no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.
skills.practice: Before each one, say the terrain elevation and add 1,500 feet, then add a margin for a shallow-dive entry [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

skills.do: Set up the right configuration (flaps and gear up), power and entry airspeed.
skills.practice: Brief the POH entry speed and VA for today's weight; stabilize at it before rolling in [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
Learn the 30° picture of the wing against the horizon and confirm it once on the attitude indicator [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

skills.do: Add power and pitch together for a smooth, coordinated climbing turn to the 90° point, bank constant, airspeed steadily falling, in either direction.
skills.practice: Constant-rate back pressure so the highest pitch arrives at the 90° reference; aileron against overbanking; more right rudder as speed drops [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

skills.do: From 90° to 180°, roll out at a constant rate, coordinated, keeping power and the pitch attitude constant.
skills.practice: Say 'freeze the nose' at 90°; time the rollout to the 180° reference; add slight back pressure to stop the nose sagging [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

skills.do: Finish the rollout at the 180° point within 10°, just above a stall airspeed, and hold that speed for a moment without stalling.
skills.practice: Know the POH power-on stall speed; have your CFI call your heading and airspeed at wings level [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

skills.do: Return to straight-and-level flight losing as little altitude as possible.
skills.practice: Lower the nose smoothly and slowly so speed builds before level flight, then set cruise power [[24:81|AFH 3-20]] [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

options: A 360° level turn at 50° of bank
A maximum performance 180° climbing turn ending wings level just above stall speed
A descending 180° turn around a point
Two 180° turns with a climb and a descent in each
quiz.why: A chandelle is a maximum performance, 180° climbing turn from about straight-and-level flight to a wings-level, nose-high attitude just above stall speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, what is the chandelle judged on?
options: Proficiency in getting maximum climb for the bank and power used, and skill
quiz.why: The standard is not the amount of altitude gained but proficiency in maximizing climb performance for the power and bank selected, and the skill shown [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

quiz.q: What bank does the commercial ACS ask for in a chandelle?
quiz.why: Establish the angle of bank at approximately 30° (ACS CA.V.C.S4). The AFH says the bank is generally 30° [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

quiz.q: Where should the flaps and retractable gear be for a chandelle?
options: Flaps up, gear down for drag
quiz.why: Before starting the chandelle, the flaps and landing gear (if retractable) should be up [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

quiz.q: In an airplane with a fixed-pitch propeller, how is the throttle set in the chandelle?
options: So as not to exceed the rpm limits
quiz.why: With a fixed-pitch propeller the throttle should be set so as not to exceed rpm limitations [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

quiz.q: In the AFH's energy model, what is the elevator?
quiz.why: The throttle is the total energy controller; the elevator distributes energy between altitude and airspeed [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

quiz.q: What happens to the overbanking tendency as airspeed decreases in the chandelle?
options: It reverses and rolls the wings level
quiz.why: As airspeed decreases, the overbanking tendency increases, so aileron is used to keep the bank fixed [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

quiz.q: Which propeller effect yaws the nose left mainly because of a high angle of attack?
quiz.why: At a high angle of attack the downward-moving blade takes a bigger bite and the nose yaws left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

quiz.q: What does the PHAK say happens if a chandelle pull-up produces more than 2 G?
options: Less altitude is gained, possibly a net loss in a low-powered airplane
quiz.why: A pull-up above 2 G will not gain as much altitude, and in low-powered aircraft it may result in a net loss [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

quiz.q: Which accident types does the AFH link to mismanaging altitude and airspeed?
options: Fuel exhaustion, bird strikes, runway incursions
Loss of control in flight, controlled flight into terrain, approach-and-landing accidents
quiz.why: Mismanaged energy is a contributing factor in the three most common fatal accident types: LOC-I, CFIT and approach-and-landing accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

final_quiz.q: A left chandelle starts on heading 090. The wings come level on heading 285 with the airspeed just above the stall. How does it compare with the ACS?
options: Fail: 15° short of the 180° point, outside ±10°
final_quiz.why: Left from 090 to 285 is only 165° of turn (90° to north, then 75° more). The target is 090 - 180 = 270, and 285 is 15° short, outside the ±10° standard (ACS CA.V.C.S7).

final_quiz.q: You are 350 lb below maximum weight. The POH lists VA at maximum weight and a lower VA for lighter weights, and gives no special chandelle speed. What entry speed fits the AFH and ACS?
options: The maximum-weight VA, for more energy
No more than the VA for today's lighter weight
final_quiz.why: Enter at the manufacturer's recommended speed, often VA or VO [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. VA decreases with weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]; above VA the airplane can reach its limit load before it stalls [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

final_quiz.q: In the second 90° the bank is coming out, which gives more vertical lift. Why does the AFH still call for a slight increase in back pressure?
options: To raise the pitch for more altitude
Because the airspeed keeps decreasing and the pitch would otherwise drop
final_quiz.why: As speed continues to decrease, a slight increase of elevator back pressure keeps the pitch attitude from decreasing [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Raising the pitch in the second 90° is a listed error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

final_quiz.q: Rolling out of a right chandelle, the ball is centered with almost no rudder. Rolling out of a left one, you need a lot of right rudder. Is something wrong?
options: Yes, the rudder is rigged wrong
No, the AFH describes exactly this difference
No, but only in low-wing airplanes
final_quiz.why: Left rollout: left adverse yaw plus left-turning tendencies need significant right rudder. Right rollout: the yaw to the right partly cancels them, so very little left rudder or less right rudder is needed [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

final_quiz.q: A friend with no parachute rides along while you practice chandelles without a CFI aboard. Your highest pitch reaches 35° nose up. What does 14 CFR 91.307 say?
options: No intentional maneuver may exceed 30° nose up relative to the horizon
It is legal if you stay below VA
final_quiz.why: With a non-crew passenger and no parachutes, no intentional maneuver may exceed 60° of bank or 30° nose up or down; exceptions are flight tests and required maneuvers given by a CFI or an ATP instructing under 61.67 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]].

final_quiz.q: Your entry is planned from a shallow dive starting 1,600 feet above the ground. What is the problem?
options: The dive may take you below 1,500 feet AGL
The bank will be too shallow
final_quiz.why: The maneuver must be performed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.C.S2). A shallow-dive entry [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] starts lower than level entry, so 100 feet of margin can be used up. Climb first.

final_quiz.q: You roll in and yank the elevator hard at VA. The airplane buffets at a speed well above the normal stall speed. What is this?
final_quiz.why: Any stall above 1 G is an accelerated maneuver stall, at a higher indicated airspeed than the 1 G stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Abrupt-maneuver stalls are more aggressive [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: Near the 180° point the stall horn sounds steadily and the airplane starts to buffet. What is the first action?
options: Hold the pitch to finish the maneuver
Forward elevator pressure to reduce the angle of attack
final_quiz.why: Recovery: forward elevator to reduce the angle of attack and stop the stall warning, level the wings, coordinate with rudder, adjust power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Stalling at any point is a listed error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

final_quiz.q: Halfway through the first 90°, you notice the bank is 42° and the nose is barely above the horizon. Which AFH errors are you making?
options: Allowing the bank to increase and flying a steep turn instead of a climbing maneuver
final_quiz.why: Allowing the bank to increase after it is set and executing a steep turn instead of a climbing maneuver are both on the AFH list [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

final_quiz.q: In the PHAK canyon example, two airplanes reverse course at 30° of bank in a 5,000-foot canyon, one at 120 knots and one at 140 knots. What is the main lesson?
options: Bank angle is the most important factor in turn room
Airspeed is the most influential factor in how much room a turn needs
final_quiz.why: The 120-knot airplane needs about 4,000 feet and makes it; the 140-knot one needs over 6,000 feet and hits the wall. Airspeed is the most influential factor, and slowing down is often better than steepening the bank [[1:138|PHAK 5-41]].

final_quiz.q: Your eyes stay on the airspeed indicator and the attitude indicator through the whole chandelle. Why is that a problem?
options: It is a listed error, and it cuts your traffic scan and your outside references
The instruments lag only in left turns
final_quiz.why: Performing by reference to the instruments rather than visual references and not scanning for traffic are both listed errors [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. In VMC the eyes on the outside world are your main orientation source [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].

final_quiz.q: At the 180° point, wings level and just above the stall, how do you return to cruise with minimum altitude loss?
options: Push the nose well below the horizon to gain speed fast
Lower the pitch smoothly and slowly so airspeed builds, then set cruise power
Hold the nose high until the stall horn stops
final_quiz.why: Once in controlled flight, reduce pitch and return to cruise [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Lower the pitch smoothly so airspeed can build; changing it too fast can cost altitude [[24:81|AFH 3-20]] (ACS CA.V.C.S8).

final_quiz.q: A student in a fixed-pitch trainer leaves the throttle at the level-flight setting for the entry speed and raises the nose with the elevator only. What does the energy model predict?
options: The same altitude gain as with climb power
Mostly a trade of airspeed for altitude, so less altitude gained for the same airspeed lost
No change in altitude at all
final_quiz.why: With thrust left about equal to drag, pitching up mostly exchanges airspeed for altitude [[24:96|AFH 4-10]] [[24:88|AFH 4-2]]; adding thrust above drag is what raises total energy [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. The AFH has power increased to the recommended setting as the climbing turn starts [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

takeaways: A chandelle is a maximum performance 180° climbing turn judged on technique, not altitude gained.
First 90°: constant 30° bank, pitch rising to its highest at 90°. Second 90°: pitch frozen, constant-rate rollout.
Commercial standard: about 30° of bank, wings level at 180° ±10°, just above a stall airspeed, no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.
Flaps and gear up; enter at the POH speed, often VA or VO, and remember VA drops with weight.
Smooth pull, moderate G: a hard pull gains less and invites an accelerated stall.
The throttle adds energy and the elevator trades airspeed for altitude; you finish with the speed tank nearly empty.
More right rudder as speed falls, especially rolling out of a left chandelle; hold the bank against overbanking.
cfi_notes: PHAK 5-36 describes the chandelle as ending at the minimum controllable airspeed [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. The AFH says just above stall speed, and later just above the power-on stall speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]; the ACS says just above a stall airspeed (ACS CA.V.C.S7). The checkride uses the ACS wording, so teach that.

Figure 10-3 box E lists 'Airspeed VS1' and 'Hold airspeed without stalling' [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. The AFH text says just above the power-on stall speed and the ACS says just above a stall airspeed (ACS CA.V.C.S7). Read the box as shorthand for 'near the stall, not stalled', not as a number to fly.

Figure 10-3 box B lists 'Neutralize ailerons' and 'Apply full power without exceeding limits'. The text says power goes to the recommended setting (rpm limits for a fixed-pitch propeller, cruise or climb for a constant-speed one), and that overbanking grows as speed drops, so aileron is used to hold the bank [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Neutral ailerons right after roll-in fits medium-bank handling [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]; expect opposite aileron later. Use the POH power setting.

The AFH lists 'initial bank too shallow resulting in a stall' [[24:215|AFH 10-6]] without explaining it. Our explanation (a slower turn rate uses up the speed before 180°) is application; demonstrate it once at altitude so the student sees it.
The sources give no pitch attitude for the 90° point. Have the student note the pitch picture that gave a good finish and write it down for that airplane and weight.

With a non-crew passenger and no parachutes, 14 CFR 91.307 limits intentional maneuvers to 30° nose up [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]]. Students practicing solo with friends aboard need to know this; flight tests and required maneuvers given by a CFI (or an ATP instructing under 14 CFR 61.67) are excepted.

The AFH energy chapter says neither the throttle nor the elevator controls altitude or airspeed by itself [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. Students raised on 'pitch for airspeed, power for altitude' find the chandelle easier to understand in energy terms; use the reservoir figure.
Fly both directions every lesson. The AFH rudder difference between left and right rollouts [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] is the most common reason a student flies one direction well and the other poorly.
Call out '90, freeze the nose' and '180, wings level' at first. Then fade the calls so the student owns the timing.
gaps: No source here gives a pitch attitude, a typical altitude gain, or a chandelle power setting for a specific airplane. Those come from the POH/AFM and your CFI.
The ACS gives no number for 'just above a stall airspeed' and no altitude allowance for 'minimum loss of altitude' (ACS CA.V.C.S7, S8). The examiner judges both.
The sources do not say how much to lead the rollout or exactly when, only that it is a constant rate from 90° to 180° [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
No source here gives a formula for VA at a lower weight; the PHAK only says it decreases, with a 100 knot versus 90 knot example [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
The sources say rpm and power fall as altitude increases [[24:80|AFH 3-19]] but do not quantify how density altitude changes chandelle performance.

activities.title: Find each point of the chandelle
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on an airplane.

activities.title: First 90° or second 90°?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap the half of the chandelle where it belongs.

items.t: Power added to the recommended setting
Bank continuously decreasing at a constant rate
Wings come level just above stall speed
Right rudder is greatest, especially in a left chandelle

activities.title: Work the chandelle numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your airplane stalls at 50 knots wings level. What is its stall speed in a level, coordinated 30° bank?
items.why: Load factor = 1 / cos 30° = 1 / 0.866 = 1.155. Square root = 1.075. 50 x 1.075 = 53.7 knots. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

items.q: Your airplane stalls at 50 knots wings level. You yank the entry pull-up up to 2 G, the load factor the PHAK names for a chandelle pull-up. What is the stall speed at 2 G?
items.why: Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. Square root of 2 = 1.414. 50 x 1.414 = 70.7 knots. Above 2 G the chandelle gains less altitude anyway [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]], so a smooth pull keeps the stall speed down.

items.q: What is the turn radius at 105 knots TAS and 30° of bank?
Same 30° bank, but the speed has dropped to 60 knots TAS. What is the radius now?
items.why: R = 3,600 / 6.501 = 554 ft. Slower at the same bank means a smaller radius [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]] [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

items.q: A left chandelle starts on heading 030. On what heading should the wings come level?
items.why: Left turn of 180°: 030 - 180 = -150, plus 360 = 210. The ACS allows ±10°, so 200 to 220 (ACS CA.V.C.S7).

items.q: At entry you are at 105 knots TAS in a 30° bank. If the speed stayed at 105 knots, how many seconds would the first 90° of turn take?
items.why: ROT = 1,091 x tan 30° / 105 = 1,091 x 0.5774 / 105 = 6.0° per second [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. 90 / 6.0 = 15 seconds. Application: in a real chandelle the speed falls, so the turn rate rises and the 90° point comes a little sooner.

activities.title: True or false: torque, P-factor and slipstream
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: To the pilot, 'torque' is made of four parts: torque reaction, corkscrew slipstream, gyroscopic action and P-factor.
The corkscrewing slipstream has its strongest effect at high forward speed and low propeller speed.
cards.why: False. It is strongest at high propeller speed and low forward speed, as in takeoffs and approaches to power-on stalls [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

cards.s: Built-in compensation for torque is usually set for cruising speed.
cards.why: True. The compensating factors are generally set for cruise, where the airplane spends most of its time [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

cards.s: In a climb, torque tends to roll the airplane to the left.
cards.why: True. Torque and P-factor cause the airplane to roll and yaw left, countered with right rudder and aileron [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

cards.s: P-factor gets weaker as the angle of attack increases.
cards.why: False. A higher angle of attack makes the downward blade's bite bigger, so P-factor grows [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

cards.s: Near the 1 G stall, more right rudder pressure is needed in slow flight than at higher speeds.
cards.why: True. The closer to the 1 G stall, the more right rudder is required [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

activities.title: Put the chandelle in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Flaps and gear up, clear the area, and check you are high enough
Establish the POH entry speed, often VA or VO
Roll smoothly into a coordinated turn of about 30°
Smooth back pressure at a constant rate while adding power
Reach the highest pitch at the 90° point, bank still constant
Hold the pitch and roll out at a constant rate, adding right rudder as needed
Wings level at 180°, just above the stall, held for a moment
Lower the nose smoothly to straight-and-level flight

activities.title: Match the mistake to the result
activities.intro: Tap a mistake, then the result the AFH links to it.

pairs.l: Pitch at the 90° point set too low
pairs.r: Airspeed never comes down to just above the stall

pairs.l: Pitch at the 90° point set too high
pairs.r: The airplane may stall before the maneuver is done
Wings come level before the 180° point
The turn goes past 180° as the wings come level

activities.title: A chandelle, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are practicing for your commercial checkride with your CFI in a high-wing trainer with a fixed-pitch propeller. You are light today. The ground below is about 1,200 feet MSL and you arrive at 2,600 feet MSL.

steps.s: Your CFI says 'Left chandelle when ready.'
options: Climb to at least 2,700 feet MSL plus a margin, then clear the area
Descend to gain entry speed, then roll in
Ask ATC for traffic and roll in
steps.why: 2,600 - 1,200 = 1,400 feet AGL, below the 1,500 feet AGL floor (ACS CA.V.C.S2). Climb, then clear with turns and spoken calls [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]] [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

steps.s: You are at the entry altitude. What speed do you set up?
options: The maximum-weight VA, since faster is more energy
The POH entry speed, not above VA for today's weight
Best rate of climb speed, VY
steps.why: Enter at the manufacturer's recommended speed, often VA or VO [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]; VA drops with weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

steps.s: Sixty degrees into the turn, the bank has crept to 36° and the nose is still coming up.
options: Leave it; more bank means more turn
Hold the bank back to about 30° with opposite aileron, keep the pitch coming up
steps.why: The overbanking tendency increases as speed drops; aileron holds the bank fixed until 90° [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Letting the bank increase is a listed error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

steps.s: You reach the 90° point at your highest pitch attitude.
options: Keep raising the pitch to gain more altitude
Hold the pitch and begin a slow, constant-rate, coordinated rollout
Lower the nose to keep speed
steps.why: From the 90° point, hold the pitch and begin a slow, coordinated constant-rate rollout so the wings are level at 180° [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

steps.s: At 170° the airplane is slow, yawing left, and you feel pushed sideways. The stall horn chirps.
options: Add right rudder to coordinate and avoid more back pressure
Add left rudder to help the turn
Pull harder to finish at exactly 180°
Roll quickly back into the bank
steps.why: Rolling out of a left chandelle needs significant right rudder at the slowest point [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Uncoordinated near the stall risks a cross-control stall [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]; the ACS wants just above the stall, not a stall (ACS CA.V.C.S7).
